chapter_summary:
As data travels across a network, it often encounters various devices that help direct it to its destination. Three fundamental devices for this purpose are hubs, switches, and routers, each operating at a different layer of the OSI model and serving distinct functions. Understanding their differences is crucial for designing and troubleshooting effective networks. A **hub** is the simplest of these devices, operating at Layer 1 (the Physical Layer). It's essentially a multi-port repeater: when it receives a signal on one port, it regenerates that signal and sends it out to all other ports. This means all devices connected to a hub share the same bandwidth and are part of a single collision domain. In a collision domain, if two devices try to transmit data simultaneously, their signals collide, requiring both devices to retransmit. Hubs are largely obsolete in modern networks due to their inefficiency and tendency to create network congestion, but understanding their basic "broadcast to all" behavior helps appreciate the advancements in network technology.

Moving up to Layer 2 (the Data Link Layer), we find the **network switch**. Unlike a hub, a switch is an intelligent device that learns the MAC addresses of devices connected to its ports and stores them in a MAC address table (also known as a Content Addressable Memory or CAM table). When a switch receives a frame, it examines the destination MAC address in the frame header. If the destination MAC address is in its table, the switch forwards the frame only to the specific port where that device is located. If the MAC address is unknown, the switch floods the frame out all ports (except the one it came in on), similar to a hub, but it then learns the source MAC address from the response. This intelligent forwarding creates separate collision domains for each port, significantly reducing collisions and improving network performance compared to a hub. Switches also provide full-duplex communication, meaning devices can send and receive data simultaneously. Advanced switches can also implement Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs), which logically segment a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains, enhancing security and network management.

The most sophisticated of these three devices is the **router**, which operates at Layer 3 (the Network Layer). Routers are designed to connect different networks (e.g., your home network to the internet, or different departments within a large organization). Their primary function is to forward packets between these distinct networks based on IP addresses. When a router receives a packet, it examines the destination IP address and consults its routing table. The routing table contains information about network paths and determines the best next hop for the packet to reach its final destination. Routers are responsible for creating and maintaining separate broadcast domains. Each interface on a router typically connects to a different network segment, and broadcasts are confined within their respective segments, preventing them from flooding the entire network. This segmentation is crucial for scalability and security in larger networks. Routers use routing protocols (like OSPF or EIGRP, or simply static routes) to dynamically learn about network paths or to be manually configured.

To illustrate the impact on network domains: a hub creates one large collision domain and one large broadcast domain. A switch breaks up the collision domain into many smaller ones (one per port), but still operates within a single broadcast domain (unless VLANs are configured). A router, by definition, separates broadcast domains; each interface on a router represents a boundary between broadcast domains. A common mistake for beginners is to confuse a switch with a router, or to use a hub when a switch is needed. Using a hub in a modern network will lead to severe performance issues. Another mistake is misconfiguring routing tables, leading to packets being dropped or taking inefficient paths. For example, if a router's default gateway is misconfigured, it won't be able to reach the internet. Troubleshooting often involves checking the MAC address table on switches (`show mac address-table` on Cisco devices) to ensure devices are learned correctly, and checking routing tables on routers (`show ip route`) to verify paths to destination networks. Safety notes primarily revolve around proper power cycling and ensuring devices are in well-ventilated areas to prevent overheating.

screens.title: Hubs, Switches, and Routers
screens.subtitle: How basic network devices direct traffic and shape collision and broadcast domains

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how three fundamental devices — hubs, switches, and routers — move data through a network and why each matters. We'll begin with the simplest device, the hub, its behavior at the physical layer, and why its broadcast-to-all design creates a single collision domain that can severely reduce performance. Then we'll explore switches at the data link layer: how they learn MAC addresses, forward frames to specific ports, create separate collision domains per port, and optionally implement VLANs to divide broadcast domains. Finally we'll examine routers at the network layer, how they forward packets by IP using routing tables, and how each router interface forms a boundary between broadcast domains. Along the way you'll see practical troubleshooting cues: what to check on a switch's MAC address table and what a router's routing table tells you about reachability. By the end of this lesson you will be able to choose the right device for typical scenarios, understand the domain boundaries each device creates, and apply simple commands to verify device behavior. Consider why a hub still appears in teaching examples: its simplicity helps us contrast targeted forwarding versus blind broadcasting. Keep that contrast in mind as you move into real-world design decisions.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Hubs broadcast to all ports (Layer 1), switches forward frames by MAC to ports (Layer 2) and reduce collisions, and routers forward packets by IP between separate broadcast domains (Layer 3).

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish hub, switch, and router functions in the OSI model and use basic commands to verify device behavior. First, you'll identify each device by its operational layer and forwarding behavior, and explain why hubs create a single collision domain while switches and routers change domain boundaries. Second, you'll describe how a switch learns MAC addresses and uses a MAC address table to forward frames efficiently, and why full-duplex ports reduce collisions. Third, you'll explain how a router forwards packets by IP using a routing table, and how each router interface separates broadcast domains. Finally, you'll practice inspecting MAC and IP information on a host and locate the default gateway and ARP entries. Each objective emphasizes practical checks and common mistakes so you can both design simple networks and troubleshoot basic connectivity problems. These skills matter because they let you choose the right device to reduce congestion, keep broadcasts contained, and make sure packets follow efficient paths between networks.

narration.text: These additional objectives focus on hands-on checks and avoiding common mistakes. screens.title: Hubs — Layer 1 repeaters and broadcast behavior
screens.subtitle: What a hub does, why it creates collisions, and when it's inappropriate

narration.text: A hub is the simplest network device and operates only at the Physical layer, meaning it does not inspect frames or addresses. When a hub receives an electrical signal on one port, it regenerates and sends that signal to every other port. This means every connected device shares the same bandwidth and lives in a single collision domain. A collision domain is a set of devices where two devices transmitting at the same time can cause their signals to collide, forcing retransmission and reducing effective throughput. Consider a small office using a ten-port hub: when multiple users send data simultaneously, collisions become frequent and performance drops noticeably. Hubs are largely obsolete in modern networks for this reason, but the hub example is important because it illustrates the baseline behavior of blind broadcasting. A common misconception is that hubs increase traffic reliability by repeating signals; in reality they increase contention and do not direct traffic intelligently. Key practical takeaway: if you want each port to avoid competing directly with all others, replace a hub with a switch. Think about whether your network traffic patterns require isolation per port — if so, a hub is not appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Hub takeaway
keyIdea.text: Hubs blindly broadcast electrical signals to all ports, creating a single collision domain and shared bandwidth for all connected devices.

content.html:
Core Concept

Hub: Layer 1 repeater

A hub regenerates a physical signal to all ports and does not inspect MAC or IP addresses. All attached devices share a single collision domain and bandwidth.

Behavior
Receives signal on one port, repeats to all others; no learning or forwarding intelligence.
Misconception
Regenerating signals does not equal directed delivery — hubs increase collisions rather than resolving them.
Example
Imagine ten workstations and a server plugged into a hub. When two users print or copy large files at the same time, frames collide and both hosts must retransmit. The server's transfers slow for everyone.
Key takeaway
Why it matters

Hubs are inappropriate where multiple devices transmit concurrently; modern LANs use switches to reduce collisions and improve throughput.

Check your understanding
  • Does your network suffer when many users transfer large files? A hub would worsen it.
  • If you need port-by-port isolation, a hub cannot provide it.

screens.title: Collision domain explained
screens.subtitle: What a collision domain is, how collisions happen, and how devices change domain size

narration.text: A collision domain is a network segment where multiple devices can interfere with each other's transmissions because they share the same medium. Collisions occur when two devices transmit at the same time and their signals overlap. When a collision happens, the frames are corrupted and both devices must retransmit, which reduces effective throughput. Hubs create a single large collision domain because every transmission is repeated to all ports. By contrast, when a switch is used, each switch port becomes its own collision domain in full-duplex mode, which prevents collisions between different ports altogether. That difference is important to understand for network performance: in environments with many simultaneous transmitters, reducing the collision domain size is essential to maintain throughput. A common misconception is to confuse collision domains with broadcast domains; they are related but different: collisions are a physical layer contention problem, while broadcast domains are about whether broadcast frames are forwarded at the data link layer. When troubleshooting slow LAN performance, ask whether devices share a collision domain and whether switching or upgrading to full-duplex ports will resolve the issue. Reflect: if you consistently observe retransmissions under load, the collision domain is a likely culprit.

keyIdea.title: Collision domain
keyIdea.text: A collision domain is where two simultaneous transmissions can collide; switches reduce collisions by isolating ports into separate collision domains.

content.html:
Definition

Collision domain

A collision domain contains devices whose frames can collide if transmitted at the same time. Collisions force retransmissions and lower throughput.

Cause
Simultaneous transmissions on the same physical medium.
Resolution
Use switches with separate ports and full-duplex links to eliminate collisions between hosts.
Concrete example
A shared hub with 8 workstations will force all traffic over the same medium. If two users copy files at once, collisions occur and throughput drops. Replace the hub with a switch and each port becomes its own collision domain, allowing simultaneous transfers without collisions.
Misconception check
Collision domains are not the same as broadcast domains; they are about simultaneous access, not reachability of broadcast frames.
Key takeaway
To fix frequent retransmits, reduce collision domains with switching and full-duplex connections.

screens.title: Switches and MAC address tables
screens.subtitle: How switches learn MAC addresses and forward frames to specific ports

narration.text: A switch operates at Layer 2 and maintains a MAC address table — often called a CAM table — which maps MAC addresses to physical switch ports. When a frame arrives, the switch reads the destination MAC address. If that MAC is in the table, the switch forwards the frame only to the port learned for that address. If the MAC is unknown, the switch floods the frame out to all ports except the ingress port, which is similar to a hub, but the switch will learn the source MAC from any reply and populate the table for future directed forwarding. This learning behavior significantly reduces unnecessary traffic and creates separate collision domains per port. A concrete example: when Host A sends to Host B on a switched LAN, the switch forwards the frame only to Host B's port once it has learned Host B's MAC, rather than broadcasting to every port. A common misconception is to think switches forward by IP; they do not — switches forward frames by MAC addresses. That distinction matters when you design and troubleshoot: a mislearned MAC, aging entries, or a port security restriction can cause unexpected flooding. The key takeaway is that the MAC address table is the switch's decision-making map; keeping it healthy yields efficient, low-collision networks.

keyIdea.title: Switch takeaway
keyIdea.text: Switches learn and use MAC address tables to forward frames to specific ports, reducing unnecessary traffic and collisions.

content.html:
Definition

MAC address table (CAM)

The switch maps layer‑2 addresses to physical ports. This enables targeted forwarding and reduces unnecessary traffic on the LAN.

Learning
Switch records source MAC and ingress port when frames arrive.
Forwarding
If destination MAC known: forward to that port. If unknown: flood and learn from responses.
Example flow
Host A sends a frame to Host B. First time, switch floods because Host B's MAC is unknown. When Host B replies, the switch learns Host B's MAC and future frames go directly to Host B's port without flooding.
Key Takeaway

The MAC address table is essential to efficient forwarding; problems with learning result in flooding and extra traffic.

Troubleshooting hint
Check the switch's MAC table to confirm a host's MAC is learned on the expected port (for example, using show mac address-table on Cisco devices).

screens.title: Switch flooding and learning process
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: unknown destination flooding, response, and table update

narration.text: When a switch receives a frame with an unknown destination MAC the device follows a predictable process: first it reads the source MAC and records the source and ingress port in its MAC address table. Next, because the destination is unknown, the switch floods the frame out all ports except the port it arrived on. When the destination receives the flooded frame and replies, its reply carries the destination's MAC as the source for that return packet. The switch sees this reply and learns the destination MAC-to-port mapping, updating its MAC table so subsequent frames can be forwarded directly. This learning loop is efficient but depends on normal two-way traffic; a host that never sends will not be learned and may continue to cause flooding for inbound traffic. A common misconception is that flooding implies switch failure; flooding can be normal for unknown addresses during the learning phase. However, sustained flooding could indicate a problem such as address table exhaustion, misconfigured devices, or a device with a spoofed MAC. The practical takeaway is to observe whether flooding is transient — learning should resolve it — and if not, inspect MAC table size and look for duplicate MACs or unauthorized devices.

keyIdea.title: Learning loop
keyIdea.text: Switches flood unknown destinations, learn source addresses from replies, update the MAC table, and then forward directly on subsequent traffic.

content.html:
Process Flow

Flood, reply, learn

1 • Receive
Record source MAC and ingress port.
2 • Flood
Send to all ports except ingress when destination unknown.
3 • Reply
Destination replies, allowing learning of its MAC.
4 • Forward
Update table and forward future frames to the correct port only.
Example
If Host X is powered on but never sends traffic, the switch may never learn Host X's MAC and will flood frames intended for it. Ensure hosts generate traffic or use static entries if necessary for critical devices.
Check
Use the switch's MAC table command to confirm learning and look for port mismatches or table exhaustion which can cause prolonged flooding.

screens.title: Switch ports, full-duplex, and VLANs
screens.subtitle: How switches reduce collisions and can segment broadcast domains using VLANs

narration.text: Switches reduce collisions by creating separate collision domains per port and by supporting full-duplex communication so devices can send and receive simultaneously. Full-duplex links remove the contention that causes collisions on half-duplex physical media. Beyond per-port collision isolation, switches can also implement VLANs to create multiple broadcast domains on the same physical hardware. A VLAN is a logical grouping of ports that behave as if on the same physical LAN even if they are scattered across the switch. VLANs are important because they let administrators segment broadcast traffic and apply different security or performance policies without additional routers for every segment. For example, you might place finance and guest devices in separate VLANs so their broadcasts do not mix. A common mistake is to assume a switch automatically separates broadcast domains; without VLANs a switch remains a single broadcast domain. The practical implication is that to contain broadcast traffic you must use routers or configure VLANs on capable switches. When designing a small office network, use per-port switching for collision prevention and add VLANs only when you need logical separation of broadcast traffic and policy enforcement.

keyIdea.title: VLAN & duplex
keyIdea.text: Switch ports isolate collision domains; full-duplex removes collisions. VLANs provide logical broadcast domain segmentation on a single switch.

content.html:
Comparison

Full-duplex vs half-duplex

Full-duplex lets a port send and receive simultaneously, eliminating collisions. Half-duplex shares the medium and can produce collisions without switching mechanisms that prevent them.

Why use full-duplex
Improves throughput and removes collision-based retransmits on switched links.

VLANs and broadcast domains

VLANs let one physical switch host multiple broadcast domains logically. Devices in different VLANs cannot reach each other's broadcasts unless routed.

Example
Finance VLAN isolates broadcast announcements from a Guest VLAN, reducing unnecessary traffic and improving security.
Misconception
A switch without VLANs still has a single broadcast domain. VLANs must be configured to split broadcasts.

screens.title: Routers — Layer 3 forwarding and broadcast separation
screens.subtitle: How routers forward packets by IP and separate broadcast domains

narration.text: A router operates at Layer 3 and is designed to connect different networks or subnets. Its primary task is to forward packets between those networks by examining destination IP addresses and consulting a routing table that lists networks and next hops. Each router interface typically connects to a different network segment, and this creates natural boundaries for broadcast domains: broadcasts are confined to the network on that interface and are not forwarded across router interfaces. This separation is essential for scalability and security in larger networks. For example, a router connecting a corporate LAN to the internet will prevent local broadcasts from flooding external links, and it will route packets destined for other networks according to its routing table. Routers can learn routes dynamically through protocols like OSPF or EIGRP, or accept static routes configured by an administrator. A common mistake is to confuse switches and routers: switches forward frames by MAC, routers forward packets by IP. When a host cannot reach a different subnet, check the router's routing table and the host's default gateway. The core idea: routers create boundaries for broadcast traffic and make forwarding decisions using IP-level information.

keyIdea.title: Router takeaway
keyIdea.text: Routers forward by IP using routing tables and separate broadcast domains by interface, enabling inter-network connectivity and controlled broadcast scope.

content.html:
Definition

Router: Layer 3 forwarding

Routers examine IP addresses and consult a routing table to determine the next hop for packets. Each interface usually represents a different network and its own broadcast domain.

Example
If a workstation needs to reach another subnet, it sends traffic to its default gateway; the router then forwards the packet according to its routing table entries or default route.
Why it matters
Routers control the reachability between networks and prevent broadcasts from propagating globally. Correct routing table entries are essential for efficient and reliable forwarding.
Misconfiguration risk
A wrong default gateway on hosts or missing static routes on routers will block traffic to outside networks — check both host settings and router tables when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Routing tables and common commands
screens.subtitle: Understanding what a routing table shows and why it matters for forwarding

narration.text: A routing table lists networks the router knows how to reach and the next hop or interface to use for each destination. When a packet arrives, the router matches the packet's destination IP against entries in this table and forwards the packet toward the correct next hop. Routes can appear because an interface is directly connected, because an administrator configured a static route, or because a routing protocol taught the router about remote networks. A useful troubleshooting step is to inspect the routing table to confirm there is a path to the desired destination or at least a default route for off-network traffic. If the table lacks a route, the router will drop the packet. A practical command on many devices is show ip route, which summarizes connected, static, and learned routes. Use that output to verify that the router has a next-hop for the target network. A common misconception is to expect routers to forward unknown networks; without a route or default gateway, routers cannot perform magic. The takeaway: validate routes first when packets go missing. If a host cannot reach an external service, confirm the host's default gateway and the router's route to the service's network.

keyIdea.title: Routing table
keyIdea.text: The routing table is the router's map of destinations and next hops; missing or wrong routes cause dropped packets or inefficient paths.

content.html:
Command

show ip route (illustrative)

A routing table shows connected, static, and protocol-learned routes and the next hops or interfaces to reach them.

Router# show ip route
Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF
C 192.168.1.0/24 is directly connected, Gig0/0
S 10.0.0.0/24 [1/0] via 192.168.1.254
O 172.16.0.0/16 via 10.0.0.2, 00:00:12, FastEthernet0/1
Practical notes
Connected routes show networks attached to router interfaces. Static routes are configured by admins. Protocol routes are learned dynamically. When troubleshooting, confirm the route type and the next hop shown in the table.
Check
If external destinations are unreachable, check the host default gateway and the router's routing table for a suitable route or default entry.

screens.title: Troubleshooting: MAC table and ARP checks
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to verify whether a switch or router knows a device

narration.text: When troubleshooting local connectivity, start by confirming the host's addressing and then verify what the network devices know. First, obtain the host's MAC and IP using ipconfig on Windows or ifconfig/ip a on Mac O S and Linux. That identifies the host's physical address and default gateway. Next, use arp -a on the host to inspect the ARP cache, which maps IP addresses to MAC addresses the host knows about. If the host shows the gateway's MAC in ARP, local Layer 2 reachability is likely working. On the switch, check the MAC address table with the device's show mac address-table command to ensure the switch has learned the host's MAC on the expected port. If the MAC is absent, the switch may never have seen traffic from the host, or the entry aged out. On the router, check the routing table to confirm a valid path to the destination network. A common mistake is to blame the router when the issue is local — always confirm the host's MAC and ARP before moving to routing checks. The practical outcome is a repeatable flow: host addressing → ARP → switch MAC table → router routing table, which isolates where packets are failing to be forwarded.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot flow
keyIdea.text: Validate host MAC/IP, check ARP entries, confirm switch learned the MAC, and then inspect router routes to find where forwarding breaks.

content.html:
Step-by-step
  1. Run ipconfig /all or ip a to find the host MAC and default gateway.
  2. Run arp -a to see IP-to-MAC mappings your host knows.
  3. On the switch, run show mac address-table to find which port learned the MAC.
  4. On the router, run show ip route to confirm a route to the destination network.
Common mistake
Assuming the router is the issue before confirming local Layer 2 connectivity. If ARP or the MAC table is missing entries, fix local learning first.
Practical tip
Follow the order: host → ARP → switch → router. This isolates the problem with minimal guesswork.

screens.title: Activity: Inspect MAC, gateway, and ARP on a host
screens.subtitle: Step through ipconfig/ifconfig and arp to connect host facts to network devices

narration.text: This hands-on activity connects the theory to a practical host inspection you can run in a lab. First, identify your MAC address and IP. On Windows, run ipconfig /all and note the Physical Address under your active adapter. On Mac O S or Linux, ip a or ifconfig shows the ether or link/ether entry. Next, identify the default gateway in the same output — this is usually the router's IP on your local network. Then check the ARP cache with arp -a to see which IPs your host has recently resolved to MAC addresses. Reflection: the ARP cache maps layer 3 addresses to layer 2 addresses, so finding the router's MAC there confirms local reachability to the gateway. If you don't find the gateway's MAC in ARP, you likely have a local link issue or wrong gateway setting. Use this flow to confirm whether the switch should have learned the host's MAC and whether the router is reachable on the local subnet. This practical check helps you quickly decide if you should inspect switch MAC tables or router routing tables next.

keyIdea.title: Activity takeaway
keyIdea.text: Running ipconfig/ifconfig and arp -a connects host-level addresses to switch and router state and pinpoints where learning or routing may fail.

content.html:
Activity

Inspect your host

Use host commands to find MAC, IP, default gateway, and ARP entries. Then relate those to the switch and router tables.

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : yourdomain.local
   Description . . . . . . . . . . : Realtek PCIe GbE Family Controller
   Physical Address. . . . . . . . : 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E  <-- Your MAC Address
   DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . : Yes
   Autoconfiguration Enabled . . . : Yes
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.100(Preferred)
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1       <-- Your Router's IP
Reflection
Why is the MAC called physical? Because it identifies the network interface at Layer 2, not a logical IP address configured at Layer 3.
Common error
Failing to find the gateway in ARP often means a wrong gateway address or a local link problem; don't jump to routing checks first.

screens.title: Typical mistakes and assessment examples
screens.subtitle: Common deployment errors and how to reason through assessment questions

narration.text: Two common assessment scenarios highlight the differences among hubs, switches, and routers and the mistakes learners often make. First scenario: a small office uses a 10-port hub and experiences severe congestion when many users access the server. The primary issue is that the hub creates a single collision domain, causing frequent collisions and retransmissions; replacing the hub with a Layer 2 switch separates ports into collision domains and reduces collisions. A common wrong choice is suggesting a router instead — routers separate broadcast domains, not collisions, and are not required to solve local contention. Second scenario: connecting two separate LANs so broadcasts don't flood each other requires a router, because routers separate broadcast domains by interface. A switch alone, unless using VLANs and routing, will not prevent broadcast traffic from traversing a single broadcast domain. When answering assessment questions, identify whether the problem is about simultaneous transmissions (collision domain) or about network reachability and broadcast containment (broadcast domain). This distinction guides the correct device choice. Ask yourself: am I fixing contention between transmitters, or am I separating distinct IP networks? That question usually leads to the right answer.

keyIdea.title: Assessment hint
keyIdea.text: Ask whether the issue is contention (collision) or network reachability/broadcast separation — that determines hub vs switch vs router choices.

content.html:
Assessment

Common mistakes

Mistake: using a hub for busy LANs
Hubs create a single collision domain causing retransmits and poor throughput; a Layer 2 switch is the correct replacement.
Mistake: confusing switch with router
Switches do not separate broadcast domains by default. Use a router or VLANs plus inter-VLAN routing to separate broadcasts between networks.
Key takeaway

Carefully identify whether a performance problem is due to collisions or improper routing and pick the device accordingly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Devices and domains
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to keep the differences clear

narration.text: Let's summarize three fundamental concepts you should remember. First, the hub is a Layer 1 device that blindly repeats signals to all ports and creates a single collision domain. Remember that hubs are largely obsolete because they increase collisions and decrease effective throughput. Second, the switch is a Layer 2 device that learns MAC addresses into a table and forwards frames only to the appropriate port when possible, which reduces collisions and improves performance. Switches still operate in a single broadcast domain unless you configure VLANs. Third, the router is a Layer 3 device that forwards packets by IP using a routing table and separates broadcast domains by interface. Routers connect distinct networks and determine the next hop for packets. Keep the practical rule: use switches to reduce collisions and routers to connect networks and contain broadcast traffic. When troubleshooting, follow host checks, ARP, switch MAC tables, and finally router routes to systematically locate the problem.

keyIdea.title: Quick summary
keyIdea.text: Hub = broadcast all (Layer 1); Switch = MAC-based forwarding and port isolation (Layer 2); Router = IP-based forwarding and broadcast separation (Layer 3).

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Three concise reminders to carry forward into troubleshooting and design.

Hub
Layer 1 repeater that broadcasts to all ports and creates one collision domain.
Switch
Layer 2 device that uses a MAC table to forward frames and isolates collision domains per port.
Router
Layer 3 device that forwards by IP using a routing table and separates broadcast domains by interface.
Summary

Use switches to reduce collisions and routers to connect networks and isolate broadcasts. Verify host addressing, ARP, switch MAC tables, and router routes when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Tables and domains
screens.subtitle: Three concise technical items you should recall

narration.text: Finally, remember these three technical items that you will use frequently. First, the MAC address table on a switch maps MAC addresses to physical ports; this table is central to efficient frame forwarding and diagnosing flooding. If a device’s MAC is not present or is on the wrong port, the switch may flood traffic or misdeliver frames. Second, the routing table on a router contains known networks and next hops; missing routes or a wrong default route are frequent causes of unreachable networks. Check the routing table when packets to other subnets fail. Third, broadcast domains define where broadcast frames travel; each router interface typically marks the edge of a broadcast domain. If you need to prevent broadcasts from reaching another group of hosts, use a router or configure VLANs with inter-VLAN routing. These three items — MAC table, routing table, and broadcast domain boundaries — form the practical toolkit you will rely on when designing and troubleshooting small networks.

keyIdea.title: Tables & domains
keyIdea.text: Keep MAC and routing tables in mind and use router interfaces or VLANs to control broadcast reachability and routing paths.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Three technical reminders for everyday troubleshooting.

MAC Address Table
Maps MAC addresses to switch ports; essential for targeted frame forwarding and diagnosing flooding.
Routing Table
Contains destinations and next hops; missing routes cause dropped packets or reliance on a default route.
Broadcast Domain
Logical area where broadcasts propagate; routers or VLANs are needed to contain broadcast traffic between groups.
Final takeaway

Use MAC and routing tables to verify device knowledge, and design with broadcast domain boundaries in mind to prevent unwanted traffic spread.
